props.title: Import/Export

sections.content: Michael Haneke's influence on Austrian cinema reaches its bleakest apex in Ulrich Seidl's Import/Export, a haunting examination of East-West dynamics in modern Europe. Like Haneke's Code Unknown (2000) and 71 Fragments (1994), Seidl employs clinical distance and parallel narratives to expose economic disparities. The film follows two mirrored journeys: an Ukrainian nurse migrating west to Austria, and an Austrian security guard heading east for work. Seidl's documentary background shapes his unflinching style, capturing both the sterile halls of Viennese hospitals and the crumbling Soviet-era apartments with the same merciless gaze.

sections.content: Seidl's approach builds on a tradition of Austrian filmmakers examining social issues through stark realism. Dog Days (2001) and Paradise: Love (2012) continue his exploration of bodies, power, and exploitation. The film's shocking moments - particularly in the geriatric ward sequences - recall similar provocations in Funny Games (1997), but Seidl grounds them in documentary authenticity rather than meta-commentary. The parallel structure emphasizes how economic migration creates mirror-image indignities on both sides of the former Iron Curtain.

The film's formal rigor places it within the Berlin School movement, alongside works like The Marriage of Maria Braun (1979) and Head-On (2004). Seidl's static compositions and long takes create a sense of surveillance, forcing viewers to confront uncomfortable realities about labor, migration, and exploitation in contemporary Europe. Like 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days (2007), the film depicts Eastern Europe's transition with unflinching attention to personal costs. SUBHEAD: Post-Soviet Cinema and Migration

sections.content: Import/Export emerged during a crucial period of European cinema examining post-Soviet migration and identity. Films like The Lives of Others (2006) looked back at the divided past, while Eastern Promises (2007) explored criminal networks exploiting East-West movement. Seidl's film stands apart by focusing on ordinary economic migrants rather than dramatic exceptions, making its critique more systemic and devastating.
